questions.question: How do Tomcat, Jetty, and Undertow differ as embedded servers in Spring Boot, and how do you switch between them?
questions.title: Embedded Server Configuration (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow)
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot defaults to embedded Tomcat but supports Jetty and Undertow by excluding the Tomcat starter and adding the desired alternative. Tomcat is the most battle-tested and widely used; Undertow offers the lowest memory footprint and highest throughput for non-blocking workloads; Jetty is a solid middle ground with a long history in OSGi and embedded use cases. All three are configured through the server.* property namespace.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the trade-offs between the three servers and can justify a server choice for a given workload.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking that switching embedded servers requires significant code changes — it is a single dependency swap because Spring Boot abstracts the server behind WebServer/ServletWebServerFactory interfaces.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that for reactive WebFlux applications Netty is the default (not Tomcat), and explain how to customise the server via WebServerFactoryCustomizer for things like connection pooling, thread counts, and SSL configuration.

sections.title: Switching Embedded Servers Is a Dependency Swap — But Choosing the Right One Isn't Trivial
sections.content:
The common misconception is that switching from Tomcat to Jetty or Undertow requires code changes. **It's a single dependency swap in your POM** — exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web` and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`. Spring Boot's `WebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration` detects which server is on the classpath and configures it automatically.

What's less obvious is **why you'd switch** and what each server is actually optimized for. Tomcat is the default because it's the most widely understood, has the largest ecosystem of documentation, and handles most workloads well. Jetty uses less memory under idle conditions and handles large numbers of long-lived connections (WebSocket, SSE) more efficiently. Undertow is the fastest on raw throughput benchmarks and uses non-blocking I/O by default.

For **reactive WebFlux applications, the default is Netty** — not Tomcat. Netty is an event-loop-based server designed for non-blocking I/O from the ground up, making it the natural fit for reactive stacks. You can force Tomcat or Undertow for WebFlux, but you lose the performance characteristics that make reactive programming worthwhile.

The switch itself is mechanical: in Maven, add `<exclusions>` on `spring-boot-starter-web` to remove `spring-boot-starter-tomcat`, then add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`. Spring Boot's `WebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration` detects which server's `ServletWebServerFactory` is on the classpath and auto-configures it. The key is that **all server configuration properties under `server.*` remain identical** regardless of which server is running — `server.port`, `server.ssl.*`, `server.compression.*` work the same way for all three. Only server-specific tuning (thread counts, connection queue depths, protocol options) requires server-specific configuration.

sections.title: Tomcat vs Jetty vs Undertow vs Netty — When Each Server Wins
sections.content:
The choice depends on your workload pattern, not just benchmark numbers.

| Aspect | Tomcat | Jetty | Undertow | Netty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Default for** | Spring MVC (servlet) | Manual swap | Manual swap | Spring WebFlux (reactive) |
| **I/O model** | Thread-per-request | Thread-per-request + async | Non-blocking (XNIO) | Event loop |
| **Memory at idle** | Higher baseline | Lower idle footprint | Moderate | Lowest |
| **WebSocket/SSE** | Good | Better for many connections | Good | Best |
| **Raw throughput** | Good | Good | Highest for servlet | Highest for reactive |
| **Ecosystem** | Most docs, most community support | Strong Eclipse ecosystem | Red Hat backed | Widely used in reactive |
| **When to choose** | General purpose, no reason to switch | Many idle connections, memory-constrained | Maximum servlet throughput | Reactive/WebFlux apps |

**The practical recommendation:** stick with Tomcat unless you have a measured reason to switch. Most applications are not I/O-bound enough for the server choice to matter. If you're seeing thread exhaustion under high concurrent connections, Undertow or a reactive stack with Netty is the fix.

sections.title: Programmatic Server Customization — Beyond application.properties
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Switch from Tomcat to Jetty or Undertow by excluding `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` and adding the alternative** — no code changes; Spring Boot auto-detects the server on the classpath.
- **WebFlux uses Netty by default, not Tomcat** — Netty is non-blocking and event-loop-based; Tomcat is blocking and thread-per-request; choosing between them drives the entire concurrency model.
- **`server.tomcat.max-threads` defaults to 200** — each thread handles one request; the ceiling on concurrent requests at blocking Tomcat is the thread pool size; too low causes request queuing under load.
- **SSL configuration: `server.ssl.key-store-type=PKCS12`** — use a keystore to terminate TLS at the application; in Kubernetes, prefer terminating TLS at the ingress controller or service mesh instead.
- **`server.compression.enabled=true` with `minimum-response-size`** — compresses responses above the threshold; reduce payload size for JSON-heavy APIs with no application code changes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot embeds the web server inside the JAR — Tomcat by default, with Jetty, Undertow, and Netty as alternatives. Choosing and configuring the right server affects throughput, memory usage, and the concurrency model.

**Switching servers**
- Exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web` and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`
- Spring Boot auto-detects the server implementation on the classpath — no code changes required
- WebFlux applications use Netty by default; Netty is non-blocking and handles thousands of concurrent connections on a small thread pool; Tomcat uses one thread per request

**Key Tomcat settings**
- `server.tomcat.max-threads=200` (default) — the maximum number of simultaneous requests; increase for high-concurrency workloads, but each thread consumes memory
- `server.tomcat.accept-count` — the queue depth when all threads are busy; requests beyond this are rejected

**Common configuration**
- `server.port=8080`, `server.compression.enabled=true`, `server.ssl.key-store` — configured via `application.properties` without touching code

The decision between Tomcat and Netty is architectural: blocking I/O with Tomcat suits traditional request-response Spring MVC; non-blocking event-loop Netty suits reactive WebFlux. Do not mix — using a blocking call inside a Netty event loop blocks the event loop and kills throughput.

beats.text: The common misconception is that switching from Tomcat to Jetty or Undertow requires code changes. It's a single dependency swap in your POM — exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat from spring-boot-starter-web and add spring-boot-starter-jetty or spring-boot-starter-undertow. Spring Boot's WebServerFactoryAutoConfiguration detects which server is on the classpath and configures it automatically. steps: Basic configuration like server.port, server.tomcat.max-threads, and server.ssl.* works through properties.
But some customizations require programmatic access to the server factory.
WebServerFactoryCustomizer<T> lets you configure the embedded server programmatically.
The generic type determines which server you're customizing — TomcatServletWebServerFactory, JettyServletWebServerFactory, or UndertowServletWebServerFactory.

``java @Bean public WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> tomcatCustomizer() { return factory -> { factory.addConnectorCustomizers(connector -> { connector.setProperty("relaxedQueryChars", "[]"); connector.setProperty("maxKeepAliveRequests", "200"); }); }; } ` This customizer gives you access to Tomcat-specific connector properties that have no equivalent in application.properties.

The key advantage is that this customizer only activates when Tomcat is the actual embedded server — if someone switches to Jetty, this bean is simply never used (assuming you guard it with @ConditionalOnClass(Tomcat.class)).
